organism: Mumps virus, a paramyxovirus related to parainfluenza and Newcastle disease viruses (antibodies against those cross-react with mumps), with a single-stranded RNA genome. It has been recovered from saliva, cerebrospinal fluid, urine, blood, semen, and breast milk, and is rapidly inactivated by formalin, ether, chloroform, heat, and ultraviolet light.
clinicalFeaturesSummary: Incubation period is usually 16-18 days (range 12-25). A nonspecific prodrome (myalgia, anorexia, malaise, headache, low-grade fever) precedes the classic presentation: parotitis (swelling of the parotid or other salivary glands, unilateral or bilateral) lasting about 5 days. Before vaccination, about 15%-24% of infections were asymptomatic or presented only with respiratory symptoms; mumps is the only known infectious cause of epidemic parotitis, and reinfection has been reported.
epidemiologySummary: Mumps is a human-only disease with no known animal reservoir and no documented carrier state, though people with asymptomatic or nonclassical infection can still transmit it. It spreads via respiratory droplets and saliva, has no seasonal pattern, and is considered infectious from 2 days before through 5 days after parotitis onset, though virus has been isolated from 7 days before to 9 days after onset, with the highest viral loads closest to onset.
secularTrendsSummary: Mumps became nationally notifiable in 1968 with about 152,000 cases reported; cases fell rapidly after vaccine introduction to fewer than 3,000 per year by 1985. A mid-1980s resurgence (about 13,000 cases in 1987), concentrated in 10-19 year-olds born before routine vaccination, contributed to the 1989 two-dose recommendation, after which cases declined steadily to fewer than 300 by 2004. Since 2006, cases have risen again - more than 1,000 per year since 2014, mostly among people who had already received 2 MMR doses, and mostly tied to close-contact-setting outbreaks (150 outbreaks and over 9,000 cases across 37 states, January 2016-June 2017).
vaccineDescription: The Jeryl Lynn strain, licensed in 1967, is the only mumps virus strain used in US vaccines; there is no single-antigen mumps vaccine available - mumps protection comes only via MMR (MMR-II) or MMRV (ProQuad). Both are live, attenuated, lyophilized, reconstituted with sterile water, given subcutaneously, and contain gelatin and neomycin with no adjuvant or preservative.
vaccinationScheduleSummary: Routine schedule is 2 doses of MMR: dose 1 at 12-15 months (minimum age 12 months), dose 2 at 4-6 years, with a minimum interval of 4 weeks (3 months for MMRV, though 4 weeks is still valid). As with measles, separate MMR and varicella vaccines are generally preferred over MMRV for the first dose in children 12-47 months because of a higher febrile-seizure risk with MMRV at that age.
evidenceOfImmunitySummary: A person can generally be considered immune to mumps without a documented vaccination if born before 1957, has serologic evidence of immunity (an equivocal result counts as negative), has laboratory-confirmed disease, or has documentation of adequate vaccination. Mumps IgG detected by a standard assay is acceptable evidence of immunity but does not reliably predict actual protection against disease - notably, during an outbreak, close contacts of a mumps patient should NOT be tested for serologic evidence of immunity, since a positive IgG titer could instead indicate acute infection.
vaccineEfficacySummary: Mumps vaccination produces a mild, noncommunicable infection. About 94% of single-dose recipients develop measurable antibody. Postlicensure studies found vaccine effectiveness of 78% after one dose and 88% after two doses.
contraindicationsSummary: A severe allergic reaction to a vaccine component or a prior dose is a contraindication, as is severe immunocompromise (malignancy, chemotherapy, congenital immunodeficiency, long-term immunosuppressive therapy, or HIV with severe immunosuppression), high-dose systemic corticosteroid therapy for 14 or more days (wait at least 1 month after stopping), a family history of congenital or hereditary immunodeficiency in a first-degree relative (unless the recipient's own immunocompetence is verified), and pregnancy (avoid pregnancy for 4 weeks after vaccination; inadvertent vaccination during pregnancy is not itself a reason to consider ending it). MMRV additionally treats HIV infection, regardless of immune status, as a contraindication. Precautions include moderate/severe acute illness, alpha-gal allergy, recent receipt of antibody-containing blood products (wait 3-11 months), a history of thrombocytopenic purpura, and an upcoming TB skin test. Egg allergy is not a reason for special precautions.
vaccineSafetySummary: Because mumps protection is delivered only via MMR or MMRV, the safety profile matches the Measles chapter's: fever of 103F or higher in 5%-15% of susceptible MMR recipients, a transient rash in about 5%, febrile seizures in roughly 1 per 3,000-4,000 MMR doses (higher with MMRV in children 12-23 months), and anaphylaxis in 1.8-14.4 cases per million doses.
vaccineStorageSummary: Follow manufacturer guidance for MMR-II and ProQuad specifically; see CDC's Vaccine Storage and Handling Toolkit for general best practices.
surveillanceSummary: Confirmation relies on RT-PCR or viral culture from buccal/oral or urine specimens; a negative result does not rule out mumps in someone with compatible symptoms. Serum IgM and IgG seroconversion testing can support a diagnosis but, unlike RT-PCR/culture, cannot confirm one on their own - false negatives are common, especially in previously vaccinated people, since their acute-phase IgG may already be elevated before a convalescent sample can show a rise. See CDC's Manual for the Surveillance of Vaccine-Preventable Diseases for state/local reporting guidance.

supplementalTopics.title: Vaccination During Mumps Outbreaks (Third Dose)
supplementalTopics.summary: During a mumps outbreak, public health authorities may identify specific groups at increased risk and recommend a third MMR dose for everyone in that group without a contraindication - including people without proof of 2 prior doses and those with presumptive evidence of immunity. No additional dose is recommended for people who have already received 3 or more doses before the outbreak.

supplementalTopics.title: Complications: Orchitis and Other Organ Involvement
supplementalTopics.summary: Orchitis is the most common complication in post-pubertal males: about 30% of unvaccinated versus 6% of vaccinated post-pubertal males develop it, with abrupt testicular swelling, tenderness, nausea, and fever; about half develop some testicular atrophy, though no study has demonstrated an actual increased sterility risk. In the prevaccine era, oophoritis and mastitis occurred in about 7% and 30% of post-pubertal women, respectively (1% or less in vaccinated women); aseptic meningitis, pancreatitis, and hearing loss occurred in up to 10%, 4%, and 4% of unvaccinated patients. In the postvaccine era, meningitis, encephalitis, pancreatitis, and hearing loss have each been 1% or less among all infected persons.

supplementalTopics.title: Vaccination of Adults and Healthcare Personnel
supplementalTopics.summary: Adults born in 1957 or later need at least 1 documented MMR dose or other acceptable evidence of immunity. Students entering college or other post-high-school institutions should have 2 documented doses. Health care personnel need 2 doses for measles/mumps immunity and 1 dose for rubella immunity - including those born before 1957 - and facilities should offer an additional outbreak-specific dose to personnel during a measles or mumps outbreak (2 doses) or rubella outbreak (1 dose).

keyPoints: Parotitis and orchitis were described by Hippocrates in the 5th century BCE; mumps virus etiology was established in 1934-1935
During World War I, only influenza and gonorrhea caused more hospitalizations among US soldiers than mumps
A successful 2-dose program drove a greater than 99% reduction in reported US mumps cases, but cases have risen again since 2006, mostly among fully vaccinated people in close-contact settings
Close contacts of a mumps patient should not be tested for immunity during an outbreak - a positive IgG titer may indicate acute infection rather than protection
No single-antigen mumps vaccine exists in the US; mumps protection comes only via MMR or MMRV
Public health authorities can recommend an outbreak-specific third MMR dose for groups at increased risk
